summary.text: An epicenter is the point on Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter, the spot underground where an earthquake or underground explosion begins.
Seismologists turn the time gap between P and S waves into a distance, and distances from at least three stations pin the epicenter to one point.
The strongest shaking is not always at the epicenter: in large quakes damage spreads along the fault rupture, and in the 2002 Denali quake it peaked about 330 km away.

facts.label: Point below it
facts.value: The hypocenter, also called the focus

facts.label: Denali quake, 2002
facts.value: Worst damage about 330 km from the epicenter

facts.label: Quakes before instruments
facts.value: Only a macroseismic epicenter can be given

items.prompt: An earthquake starts 10 km beneath a farm. Where is its epicenter?

options.label: On the ground right over that starting spot
Down at the spot 10 km below the farm
Wherever the buildings were damaged worst
At the nearest seismograph station

items.explain: The epicenter is the surface point straight above the place underground where the quake begins.

items.prompt: A single seismograph shows a quake struck 300 km away. Why can't it say exactly where?

options.label: One station can only measure a quake's size
That distance fits any point on a circle around it
Its first and second waves always arrive together
Its clock cannot time waves that far away

items.explain: One distance traces a circle of possible spots; a second station narrows it to two points and a third to one.

items.prompt: Seismologists want to pin down the exact spot a quake began. What is the fewest seismometers they need?

options.label: One
Two
Three
Five

items.explain: Each station gives a distance, and only the overlap of three distances gives a single location.

items.prompt: After a large quake, a town 200 km from the epicenter suffers the worst damage. What is the likeliest reason?

options.label: The epicenter must have been placed wrongly
Seismic waves get stronger the farther they go
The town sits directly over the quake's focus
The rupture spread along the fault toward the town

items.explain: In big quakes the rupture runs along the fault, and its direction can put the strongest shaking far from the epicenter.

items.prompt: At a station, the first jolt of a quake arrives 40 seconds before the second. What does that gap mainly tell a seismologist?

options.label: How deep the quake started
Which way the fault moved
How far away the quake was
How long the shaking lasted

items.explain: P waves arrive before S waves, and because their speeds are known, the gap between them gives the distance to the epicenter.

items.prompt: Historians want to place a quake from the year 1500, long before seismographs. What can they offer?

options.label: An exact point taken from old pendulum logs
Nothing at all, since no records can help
The worst-hit town, which is always the spot
An estimate from shaking reports and local faults

items.explain: Without instruments only a macroseismic epicenter can be given, estimated from intensity data, foreshocks and aftershocks, and known faults.
